c.tagline: Gothic cathedral city on the Seine where Monet painted and Joan of Arc died

taxi.fareNote: Official taxis are metered with a visible rooftop light; fixed supplements apply for night, Sunday, and station pickups

emergency.note: 112 works for all emergencies; 17 reaches police directly and 15 reaches the SAMU medical service

avoid.reason: Mind bags around the rail station and in crowds near the cathedral; left-bank streets are quiet and deserted after dark.

hood_desc: Vieux Rouen (the historic center) is a dense maze of half-timbered medieval houses around the Gros-Horloge and Rouen Cathedral, packed with shops, cafés, and the Place du Vieux-Marché where Joan of Arc was burned at the stake.
Saint-Marc is a lively, slightly bohemian neighborhood built around its namesake outdoor market, popular with students and known for an easygoing, multicultural feel.
Jouvenet, near the Musée des Beaux-Arts, is a quiet, well-heeled residential quarter of grand 19th-century townhouses just north of the old center.
Saint-Sever, on the left bank, centers on a large shopping mall and transit hub, offering practical, budget-friendly lodging within a short tram ride of the cathedral.
lodging: Mercure Rouen Centre Champ de Mars
ibis Rouen Centre Champ de Mars

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout France.

transit.pay: Astuce card or app tickets, single fare covers bus/tram transfers for about an hour
transit.note: Rouen's TEOR guided busway and single tramway line cover the compact city well; the historic center itself is best explored on foot

train: Direct SNCF trains from Paris Saint-Lazare, about 70-90 minutes
bus: FlixBus and BlaBlaCar Bus connect Rouen to Paris and other French cities

tip.r: Service is included by law (service compris); rounding up or leaving small change for good service is appreciated but not obligatory

food.name: Canard a la Rouennaise
food.desc: Rouen's grand old dish: a smothered duck roasted rare, then its carcass pressed to make a sauce of blood, juices and cognac. Order well in advance.

places.name: La Couronne
places.note: Inn dating to 1345 and one of the last places still pressing the duck properly; Julia Child ate here.

places.name: Les Gens Heureux
places.note: Chef Vincent Taillefer's Normandy-focused menus, from lunch prix fixe to full tasting.

places.name: L'Odas
places.note: Michelin-starred Rouen kitchen for modern Norman cooking if the classic is not available.

food.name: Sole Normande
food.desc: Channel sole poached and blanketed in a cream sauce with mussels, shrimp and mushrooms. Norman dairy meeting the coast an hour up the Seine.

places.name: La Couronne
places.note: Classical Norman repertoire served in wood-panelled dining rooms; book ahead.

places.name: Minute et Mijote
places.note: Small, consistently well-reviewed bistro doing market cooking at fair prices.

places.name: Le P'tit Bec
places.note: Long-running bistro on the prettiest street in Rouen; good-value Norman plates.

food.name: Mirliton de Rouen
food.desc: A puff-pastry tartlet filled with almond and orange-blossom cream, dusted with sugar. The city's own pastry, best eaten slightly warm.

places.name: Ma Boulangerie
places.area: Place du Vieux-Marche and Rue Armand Carrel
places.note: Widely named as the best mirliton in Rouen; two shops, both central.

places.name: Auzou
places.note: Historic Rouen patisserie and chocolatier, also home of the Larmes de Jeanne d'Arc.

places.name: Halles du Vieux-Marche
places.note: Covered market with pastry stalls; open Tuesday to Sunday mornings.

food.name: Teurgoule
food.desc: Norman rice pudding baked for five hours with milk, sugar and cinnamon until a dark caramelised skin forms. Humble, sweet and very filling.

places.name: Halles du Vieux-Marche
places.note: Market stalls sell teurgoule by the terrine, often still warm from the oven.

places.name: Marche Saint-Marc
places.note: Big Sunday morning market where Norman producers bring teurgoule and cider.

places.name: La Couronne
places.note: Keeps traditional Norman desserts including teurgoule on the menu.

food.name: Neufchatel and Norman Cheeses
food.desc: The heart-shaped Neufchatel comes from the Pays de Bray just north of Rouen. Eat it with Camembert, Livarot and Pont-l'Eveque on one board.

places.name: Halles du Vieux-Marche
places.note: Cheesemongers here carry all four Norman AOP cheeses at proper ripeness.

places.name: Marche Saint-Marc
places.note: Sunday farmers market with producers selling raw-milk Neufchatel direct.

places.name: La Couronne
places.note: Full Norman cheese trolley if you would rather taste them at the end of a meal.

food.name: Sucre de Pomme and Larmes de Jeanne d'Arc
food.desc: Rouen's two confections: clear apple-sugar sticks made since the 1600s, and chocolate almonds named for Joan of Arc, burned in the city in 1431.

places.name: Auzou
places.note: Creator of the Larmes de Jeanne d'Arc; the definitive Rouen sweet shop since 1857.

places.name: Halles du Vieux-Marche
places.note: Confectionery stalls sell sucre de pomme in tins that travel well.

places.name: Confectioners around the cathedral
places.note: The pedestrian street between cathedral and market is lined with sweet shops.

food.name: Cidre de Normandie
food.desc: Farmhouse apple cider poured from a bottle or a bolee, from bone-dry brut to soft doux. The standard partner for Norman food, and low in alcohol.

places.name: Le P'tit Bec
places.note: Bistro serving Norman cider by the jug alongside galettes and regional plates.

places.name: Marche Saint-Marc
places.note: Sunday market producers sell farm cider and perry straight from the orchard.

places.name: La Couronne
places.note: Proper Norman cider list to drink with the duck instead of wine.

food.name: Calvados and Pommeau
food.desc: Apple brandy aged in oak, drunk as a digestif or as the mid-meal trou normand. Pommeau blends unfermented juice with calvados for a softer aperitif.

places.name: La Couronne
places.note: Deep calvados selection served the traditional way at the end of the meal.

places.name: L'Odas
places.note: Michelin-starred room with a curated Norman spirits list and knowledgeable staff.

places.name: Halles du Vieux-Marche
places.note: Stalls selling estate calvados and pommeau by the bottle to take home.

landmarks: Cathédrale Notre-Dame de Rouen (Rouen Cathedral)
The soaring Gothic cathedral immortalised in Monet's series paintings, once the world's tallest building and resting place of Richard the Lionheart's heart.
Gros-Horloge
A gilded 14th-century astronomical clock mounted on a Renaissance arch straddling Rouen's main street, one of Europe's oldest working clock mechanisms.
Place du Vieux-Marché and Église Sainte-Jeanne-d'Arc
The square where Joan of Arc was burned in 1431, now marked by a sweeping modern church whose roof evokes flames and an upturned ship.
Aître Saint-Maclou
A rare medieval plague ossuary courtyard, its half-timbered galleries carved with macabre skulls, bones and gravediggers' tools from the Black Death era.
Église Saint-Maclou
A jewel of Flamboyant Gothic architecture whose lace-like porch and carved Renaissance doors rise dramatically amid Rouen's finest half-timbered lanes.
Abbatiale Saint-Ouen
A monumental 14th-century abbey church rivalling the cathedral in scale, celebrated for its radiant stained glass and legendary Cavaillé-Coll organ.
Palais de Justice
A flamboyant late-Gothic law-courts palace, among France's grandest civil medieval buildings, sheltering the 12th-century Jewish monument known as the Maison Sublime.
Musée des Beaux-Arts de Rouen
One of France's richest provincial art museums, hung with Caravaggio, Velázquez and a superb Impressionist collection led by Monet's cathedral canvases.
Historial Jeanne d'Arc
An immersive multimedia journey through Joan of Arc's trial and myth, staged in the very archbishop's palace where her case was heard and revised.
Panorama from Côte Sainte-Catherine
The hillside viewpoint painted by Monet and Turner, where Rouen's spires and Seine loops spread out in Normandy's most celebrated cityscape.

train.note: No international trains. Rouen Rive-Droite has frequent Intercités services to Paris Saint-Lazare in about 70 minutes and trains down the Seine valley to Le Havre and Dieppe. For Eurostar you change in Paris between Saint-Lazare and Gare du Nord. SNCF advance fares open around six months ahead.

intl.to: London (UK) & across Europe - via the Dieppe or Calais crossing

bus.note: Coaches stop near the station. FlixBus and BlaBlaCar Bus run to Paris, Caen and onward to London using the Channel crossing, where you get off for UK immigration - carry your passport. Local Nomad buses serve Étretat and the Normandy coast.

ferry.note: Rouen is a working river port on the Seine but has no scheduled passenger ferry - cruise ships call and small chain ferries cross the river downstream at Duclair and Jumièges. The Channel crossings are at Dieppe, about an hour north, with DFDS sailing to Newhaven, and at Le Havre and Ouistreham for Brittany Ferries.

half.name: Giverny
half.blurb: Claude Monet's house and water-lily gardens lie about an hour away, the setting he painted repeatedly during the last decades of his life.

half.name: Étretat
half.blurb: Chalk cliffs and natural rock arches rise from the sea about an hour and a half away, a stretch of coast painted by Monet and Courbet.

half.name: Honfleur
half.blurb: A picturesque harbor town about an hour and 20 minutes away has a slate-fronted old port and the wooden Sainte-Catherine church.

half.name: Jumièges Abbey
half.blurb: The roofless ruins of a Benedictine abbey about 30 minutes away rise beside a bend in the Seine, founded in the 7th century.
